sources.title: Informed Consent to Treatment in Psychiatry
sources.version: Canadian Psychiatric Association position paper, approved by the CPA Board of Directors 21 May 2014; published in The Canadian Journal of Psychiatry 2015;60(4):1-11
sources.locator: Sections 'The Ethical Foundations of Consent', 'The Process and Procedure of Consent', 'Consent Decisions Must Be Voluntary', 'Consent Decisions Must Be Informed', and 'Mentally Capable'. Used for the general consent-as-process model, not for current jurisdiction-specific rules; the association's own convention treats position papers older than five years as requiring review, and no re-endorsement was verifiable through this project's permitted routes.
sources.license: © Copyright 2015, Canadian Psychiatric Association; reproduction requires written permission from the association. Citation-only factual reference.

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Only bounded facts were taken: that consent is described as a continuing process reviewed and renewed rather than an instant; that the consent form or note is evidence of a discussion at a moment and is not the consent itself; that consent does not bind a person to proceed and does not remove the right to withdraw at any time; the list of matters requiring disclosure including the identity of the person providing the treatment; the circumstances the paper names as compromising voluntariness; the decision-specific account of capacity and the statement that mental illness, disagreement, and unwise choices do not by themselves establish incapacity; and that consent requirements differ between Canadian provinces and under Quebec civil law. No wording, case citation text, table, heading sequence, or document structure was copied or adapted, and every example, exchange, and table in the lesson is this lesson's own.

sources.title: Mandatory and permissive reporting laws: obligations, challenges, moral dilemmas, and opportunities
sources.publisher: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians Open
sources.locator: Section 1.1 'What are mandatory reporting laws and why are they necessary?' and section 1.4.2 'Duty to warn or protect: Tarasoff laws'
sources.license: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 as displayed on the article record; NonCommercial and NoDerivatives place it outside the project's reuse set, so facts only.

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Only bounded facts were taken: that reporting duties set aside patient confidentiality and autonomy in defined circumstances; that United States duty-to-warn and duty-to-protect obligations after Tarasoff are mandatory in roughly 27 to 33 states, permissive in roughly 9 to 11, and absent from statute in roughly 6 to 13, the ranges reflecting disagreement about classification; and that clinicians are expected to be familiar with the law of the state in which they practise. No wording, table, case discussion, or document structure was copied or adapted.

sources.title: Assessment of Patient Nondisclosures to Clinicians of Experiencing Imminent Threats
sources.locator: Results: nondisclosure among respondents reporting imminent threats (613 of 1292 and 581 of 1453) and the ranked reasons for nondisclosure
sources.license: © 2019 Levy AG et al., JAMA Network Open; open-access article distributed under the terms of a Creative Commons Attribution licence as displayed on the article record.

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Only bounded facts were taken: the two survey sample sizes and populations; that among respondents reporting depression, suicidal ideation, abuse, or sexual assault, 47.5% and 40.0% reported withholding at least one of them from a clinician; and the ranked reasons given, including embarrassment, not wanting to be judged or lectured, not wanting difficult follow-up, and not wanting the information in the medical record at 57.1% and 52.7%. sources.locator: Results: 370 participants, 185 from Psychiatry and 185 from Pediatrics; the 75% and 31% figures for the psychiatry group excluding respondents who did not remember; and the findings on discomfort and disclosure of intimate problems

sources.title: Privacy and Confidentiality in Emergency Medicine: Obligations and Challenges
sources.publisher: Emergency Medicine Clinics of North America
sources.locator: Sections 'Design', 'Observers', 'Visitors', and 'Communication among health care providers'
sources.license: Copyright © 2006 Elsevier Inc., all rights reserved; the record is publicly readable through PubMed Central. Citation-only factual reference.

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Only bounded facts were taken: that curtains provide visual separation while leaving conversations audible and that staff conversation in open areas is a routine route by which confidentiality is compromised; that many institutions treat a general admission consent as covering student observation while other writers hold that explicit consent should be sought for each observation; and that visitors should be present only with the patient's permission. No wording, table, or document structure was copied or adapted. The source is used to establish that the observer-consent question is contested and is explicitly dated in the lesson prose.

sources.title: Do Professional Interpreters Improve Clinical Care for Patients with Limited English Proficiency? A Systematic Review of the Literature
sources.version: Health Serv Res 2007;42(2):727-754; doi 10.1111/j.1475-6773.2006.00629.x; literature searched to September 2005
sources.locator: Results across the four outcome categories of communication errors and comprehension, utilisation, clinical outcomes, and satisfaction; and the Limitations section
sources.license: © 2007 Health Research and Educational Trust; no open-content licence displayed on the record. Citation-only factual reference.

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Only bounded facts were taken: that 28 studies were reviewed across four outcome categories; that professional interpreters were associated with fewer communication errors and better comprehension, service use, clinical outcomes, and satisfaction than ad hoc interpreters such as family members and untrained bilingual staff; and the review's own limitations, including that most included studies were observational and conducted in the United States. No wording, table, or figure was copied or adapted, and no numerical error rate from the review is reproduced in the lesson.

sources.title: International variations in primary care physician consultation time: a systematic review of 67 countries
sources.version: BMJ Open 2017;7(10):e017902; doi 10.1136/bmjopen-2017-017902; literature searched 1946 to 2016
sources.locator: Abstract Results and Conclusions; Results tables of mean consultation length by country
sources.license: CC BY-NC 4.0 as displayed on the article record; the NonCommercial condition places it outside the project's reuse set, so facts only.

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Only bounded facts were taken: that 179 studies from 111 publications covering 28,570,712 consultations in 67 countries were included; that average consultation length ranged from 48 seconds in Bangladesh to 22.5 minutes in Sweden; that 18 countries representing about 50% of the global population have five minutes or less; and the review's own limitations about reliance on averages and the absence of rural, urban, public, and private breakdowns. sources.title: Changes in Documentation After Implementing Open Notes in Mental Health Care: Pre-Post Mixed Methods Study

sources.license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence as displayed on the article record.

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Only bounded facts were taken: the design, setting, and note and patient counts; that stigmatising, controlling, demeaning, and incomprehensible language decreased while comprehensible, personal, resource-oriented, heteroglossic, and positive emotional language increased; that the interviewed clinicians said the substantive content of documentation was unchanged and described handling sensitive material through more general phrasing; and that the study has no control site.
